candidates.source_summary: Springhill Hospice in Rochdale has won three awards through the Royal Horticultural Society’s In Bloom programme, including Best Hospice Garden in the North West for 2026.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Springhill Hospice in Rochdale has won three awards through the Royal Horticultural Society’s In Bloom programme, including Best Hospice Garden in the North West for 2026. The hospice received Level 5 Outstanding, the highest rating in the Rochdale in Bloom It’s Your Neighbourhood Awards. It also received a Level 5 Outstanding Five Year Achievement Award for maintaining that standard over the five years it has entered. Springhill was named Best Hospice Garden in the North West 2026 at the North West in Bloom Awards. The regional award recognises the role hospice gardens play in providing welcoming spaces for patients, families, visitors and staff. A team of 18 volunteer gardeners maintains the grounds throughout the year. Patients and their loved ones use the gardens to sit together, spend time in quiet surroundings and enjoy the changing seasons. The grounds are also used by visitors, volunteers and staff. Claire Connely, head gardener at Springhill Hospice, said, “I couldn’t be prouder of everyone, but especially our magnificent garden team and all the marvellous things they have achieved together. “Week after week, come rain or shine, our volunteers give their time, skills and energy to care for the gardens and create something truly special for everyone who visits Springhill. “To receive three awards, and particularly to be named Best Hospice Garden in the North West, is wonderful recognition of everything they put into making our gardens what they are. They are an astonishingly beautiful and important part of Springhill, and these awards belong to every person who has played a part in creating and caring for them.” The hospice’s Business Buddies and corporate volunteers regularly contribute their time, expertise and practical help. Local people and organisations donate plant pots, coffee grounds, plants and gardening materials. The team at 3 Pitts allotment grows and donates 400 begonias each spring, which are planted throughout the hospice grounds.

candidates.source_summary: Rochdale Masters Rugby League and Mayfield Movers have raised £14,698.67 for charities and community rugby league through two walking challenges.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale Masters Rugby League and Mayfield Movers have raised £14,698.67 for charities and community rugby league through two walking challenges. Their latest walk raised £6,141.80, with three charities set to receive at least £1,500 each. Walkers set off from Ince Rose Bridge ARLFC in Wigan at 6.30am on Saturday 31 October 2026 for the 44-mile All Together Walk. The route took in 10 community rugby league clubs across Greater Manchester, passing through Leigh, Salford and Bury before the group reached Rochdale Mayfield ARLFC at 9.48pm. Volunteers and supporters helped the group during the walk, which took more than 15 hours. Rugby league clubs along the route welcomed the walkers with refreshments and encouragement. The Motor Neurone Disease Association, the Rugby League Cares Brain Health Fund and Springhill Hospice in Rochdale will each receive at least £1,500. The three charities are due to receive a combined minimum of £4,500. Rochdale Masters has committed to covering all fundraising transaction fees so that each charity receives its full allocation. The remaining proceeds will go towards developing the Rochdale Masters section and helping people stay active, socially connected and involved in rugby league. The same groups raised £8,556.87 in October 2025 by walking 52 miles from Rochdale to Blackpool. Mayfield Movers is a community walking group based at Rochdale Mayfield ARLFC, where Rochdale Masters also operates. Both groups aim to help people of different ages, backgrounds and abilities take part in physical activity, build friendships and improve their physical and mental wellbeing.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Tributes have been paid to an “outstanding” young student and talented playwright. Obesi Osi-Iyere was laid to rest this week following her death on October 28 aged just 20. She was a student at the University of Warwick after excelling in her A-levels at Cardinal Langley RC High School in Middleton. In a tribute, Cardinal Langley shared: “We received the deeply sad news that Obesi Osi-Iyere had passed away. Yesterday (Wednesday), Sixth Form staff had the privilege of attending a celebration of her life. “Obesi was an exceptional young person who had the world at her feet. She completed her Sixth Form studies in August, 2025, achieving an outstanding two A* and two A grades in mathematics, further mathematics, English language and economics. “She subsequently began studying for a BSc in mathematics, operational research, statistics and economics at the University of Warwick. “Beyond her academic excellence, Obesi was an incredibly talented and creative individual, with a passion for writing, playwriting and theatre. candidates.source_summary: Rochdale man jailed for life after murdering wife and hiding her body under the bed for two days The Manc
candidates.source_body_excerpt: He only reported the incident once the body began to smell. A man from Rochdale has been sentenced to life in prison after murdering his wife and hiding her body under the bed for two days. Having previously denied the offence, Kyle Howard appeared at Manchester Crown Court this week where he finally pleaded guilty to, and was then subsequently sentenced to life for, the murder of 44-year-old Keeley Aspinall. His sentencing comes after officers from Greater Manchester Police (GMP) responded to a report made by Howard at around 4pm on 25 May 2026, who stated that he had killed his wife in their home on Tweedale Street in Rochdale – adding that he had stabbed her to two days earlier, and was only now reporting the incident because her body was beginning to smell. When police arrived at the address, they discovered Keeley’s body concealed underneath a bed, and Howard was immediately arrested on suspicion of murder. Paramedics attended the scene along with police , but Howard was reported as telling them: “There is no point being here, I’ve done it, she’s dead, she’s been dead for two days.” After his arrest, Howard made several confessions whilst being booked into police custody – including making comments such as: “It’s her own f*cking fault”, “I’m not denying it”, and “I’ll admit it, I’m not bothered.” When questioned on the incident, Howard stated that the pair had been drinking and began to argue in the kitchen.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig has said a social landlord is running housing stock in Rochdale ‘into the ground’ following the announcement the Seven Sisters tower blocks are to be bulldozed. On Monday (November 16), Rochdale Boroughwide Housing (RBH) said it intended to demolish the 766 flats and replace them with a mix of 601 new flats and town houses. The decision brings to an end an era of uncertainty for the site, officially called College Bank. The towers were first earmarked for demolition a decade ago. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter Speaking on BBC Radio Manchester’s weekly mayoral phone in show, Ms Craig said ‘knocking down stock without a clear plan’ as to when homes would be replaced was ‘incredibly disappointing’. She added that ‘there’s a long-standing issue with the provider’ and the matter had ‘been 10 years in the making’. Around 80 households remain at Seven Sisters with the previous uncertainty leading to many tenants departing. Campaigners have fought to stop demolition ever since it was first mooted in 2016. They want to see the 1960s block refurbished instead. It comes as RBH bosses released computer-generated images showing how the site could look once the towers have been knocked down and the plot redeveloped. Ms Craig was answering the concerns from a campaigner called Mark. He said that since 2012, social housing stock Rochdale had been depleted from 13,700 units and ‘if we lose College Bank and Lower Falinge, that figure will be down to 11,000’. Ms Craig was told at a campaign meeting for residents on Wednesday evening (November 18), ‘the anger was palpable’ and that it was ‘scandalous’ that 20,000 people were on the social housing waiting list in the borough. The mayor said: “To get to a situation where a social housing provider is essentially running stock into the ground is not acceptable. I’m trying to bring together Rochdale Boroughwide Housing with the council to get them to listen to the voice of community. “I’m disappointed that this is where we’ve come to. In the middle of a housing crisis, knocking down stock without a clear plan as to when RBH is going to be able to replace those social homes that we desperately need is incredibly disappointing. “I received the notification from RBH that the decision had been made and that it was going ahead. That’s a little bit at odds from the last meeting that we had with them. “I can understand residents’ frustration on this. This has been a long fight, and I know there’s a lot of anger out there. I think there’s a long-standing issue with the provider that we’re talking about here.” RBH says it would be too expensive and would take too long to refurbish the blocks, so has opted to redevelop the site. Bosses estimate it would take 12 years to refurbish and cost £269m – around £388,000 per flat. The decision was made by RBH after more than a year of working with the ‘College Bank Task Force’, which includes the council and Greater Manchester Combined Authority. RBH said that included ‘a detailed review of all available scenarios’. Ms Craig said she would make clear to RBH that she ‘want[s] to know a clear plan’. She said her key questions to the social housing provider were: ‘when are those new homes going to be built?’ and ‘what is that commitment to people that have been moved away to come back?’. candidates.source_body_excerpt: A new approach is being trialled to tackle the misery prolific shoplifters cause on the high street. Greater Manchester has been selected for the Prolific Retail Offenders Pilot Programme which will see the most active and harmful shoplifters dealt with through coordinated action by police, probation, councils, housing services and retailers. The programme is built on evidence that a relatively small group of highly prolific individuals commits a disproportionate number of thefts from shops, causing repeated harm to shop workers and businesses. They also put a continual demand on police, courts and other public services. As well as enforcement, the pilot will tackle the causes of persistent offending, such as drug and alcohol misuse and unstable housing. The aim is to make better use of the tools and services already available, backed by extra support from government. The programme forms part of the government high streets strategy Hope on the High Street and will also look at the barriers that stop agencies stepping in when the same people cycle through the justice system again and again. Greater Manchester Police and local partners are currently drawing up plans, and decisions on where activity will focus within the force area will be made locally, based on patterns of offending. candidates.source_summary: With hundreds of families currently in temporary accommodation, the council wants to make it more suitable and cost-effective.
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Hundreds of families are currently living in temporary accommodation in Rochdale . And it comes at a huge cost to the council. Now the town hall has a £5.6m plan to make sure temporary accommodation is suitable and more cost-effective over the next four years. The local authority has devised a framework that would help them control the types of housing they offer those at risk of homelessness, who can be some of the most vulnerable in society. As of the beginning of November, there are 387 Rochdale households in temporary accommodation, according to council papers. Of these, 250 of are families with children and there 13 families in Bed & Breakfasts and five families in out of borough placements. Use of hotels and B&Bs is the most expensive provision and is also more likely not to be up to standard, a report found. A higher complexity of need for those using the council’s housing service as well as a decrease in social housing supply in the borough is what has sparked the town hall to take action. The new framework would allow the town hall to have greater oversight and influence over the local supported accommodation. This plan would see the types of accommodation into four ‘Lots’ and is estimated to cost £5.6m over four years. Lot 1 and Lot 2 would incur the largest expense at an estimated £4.9m, because they include B&Bs and nightly paid accommodation for the homeless.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Hundreds of families are currently living in temporary accommodation in Rochdale – and it comes at a huge cost to the council. Now the town hall has a £5.6m plan to make sure temporary accommodation is suitable and more cost-effective over the next four years. The local authority has devised a framework that would help them control the types of housing they offer those at risk of homelessness – who can be some of the most vulnerable in society. As of the beginning of November, there are 387 Rochdale households in temporary accommodation, according to council papers. Of these, 250 of are families with children and there 13 families in Bed & Breakfasts and five families in out of borough placements. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter The use of hotels and B&Bs is the most expensive provision and is also more likely not to be up to standard, a report found. A higher complexity of need for those using the council’s housing service as well as a decrease in social housing supply in the borough is what has sparked the town hall to take action. The new framework would allow the town hall to have greater oversight and influence over the local supported accommodation. The plan would see the types of accommodation into four ‘Lots’ and is estimated to cost £5.6m over four years. Lot 1 and Lot 2 would incur the largest expense at an estimated £4.9m, because they include B&Bs and nightly paid accommodation for the homeless. Lot 3 would contain homelessness supported accommodation and Lot 4 would be ‘supported pathway housing’ for homeless families and individuals. The framework would allow housing providers to register with the council under one of these ‘lot’ pathways and the local authority would identify whether they meet the required standards. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Campaigners fighting to save Rochdale’s College Bank flats from demolition are calling on community leaders to step in and save the landmark tower blocks. Yesterday, Rochdale Boroughwide Housing announced that demolition and redevelopment of the site is the only viable option for the 61-year-old tower blocks known as the Seven Sisters. It said refurbishing them would cost at least £269 million and take up to 12 years — estimated at £388,000 for each of the 766 flats before VAT. RBH said the renovations would add another 50 years to the lifespan of the buildings, while redevelopment would provide 601 homes in a mix of sizes, creating a minimum additional 249 bedrooms, and the properties would last “significantly longer”. Reacting to the news, Greater Manchester Tenants Union said the decision was part of a “managed decline” overseen by the housing provider — a claim RBH denies. GMTU said: “Campaigners and the wider community are very disappointed with the decision to pursue demolition by RBH. “For 10 years the tenants and leaseholders of College Bank have suffered one mistaken decision after another. “RBH claims the decision is based upon ‘a detailed review of all available scenarios’ but it has only allowed for a costing of an overpriced refurbishment plan based upon installing a second staircase in each block of College Bank (under new regulations following the Grenfell disaster).”

The decision brings to an end an era of uncertainty for the towers, actually called College Bank, which were first earmarked for demolition a decade ago. That’s because only around 80 households remain from the original 766 since the original demolition announcement 10 years ago.
